guidance: Avoid allergens such as dust, pollen, and pet dander. Use prescribed antihistamines or intranasal corticosteroids. Saline nasal rinses may help. If symptoms interfere with daily life, see an ENT specialist. Immunotherapy (allergy shots) can provide long-term relief.
precautions: Keep living spaces clean and dust-free
Use masks during high pollen seasons
Keep windows closed during pollen season

symptoms: facial pain or pressure over the sinuses
guidance: Use steam inhalation, saline nasal sprays, and stay well-hydrated. Over-the-counter decongestants may help. If symptoms persist beyond 10 days or worsen, see a doctor; bacterial sinusitis may require antibiotics. Avoid smoking and allergens.
precautions: Use a humidifier in dry environments

symptoms: chest pain that worsens with deep breathing
guidance: Consult a pulmonologist immediately if symptoms persist. Early detection through low-dose CT screening (in high-risk individuals) improves outcomes. Treatment includes surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. Free treatment is available under PMJAY for eligible patients. Smoking cessation is the most important preventive measure.
precautions: Avoid smoking and tobacco in all forms
Avoid exposure to industrial pollutants (asbestos, radon, silica)
Attend regular health screenings if high-risk (age >50, smoking history)
Maintain a healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables
Report any persistent cough or blood in sputum immediately

guidance: Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and use saline nasal sprays. Over-the-counter cold medications may relieve symptoms. Antibiotics are not effective for viral colds. Handwashing and avoiding close contact with infected persons help prevent spread.
precautions: Wash hands frequently with soap and water
Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or elbow
Use disposable tissues and dispose of them properly

symptoms: swollen lymph nodes in the neck
guidance: Gargle with warm salt water, drink warm liquids (honey and lemon tea), and use throat lozenges. If fever is high, take paracetamol. If symptoms persist >3 days, or if there is pus on tonsils, see a doctor – may need antibiotics for strep throat. Avoid spicy foods and smoking.
precautions: If you have strep, complete the antibiotic course

symptoms: feeling of a lump in the throat
guidance: Rest your voice – avoid talking and whispering (whispering strains the vocal cords). Drink warm fluids, use a humidifier, and avoid irritants (smoke, alcohol). If hoarseness lasts more than 2 weeks, see an ENT specialist. Usually self-limiting.
precautions: If vocal strain is chronic, seek voice therapy

symptoms: pain or burning in the chest (tracheal area)
guidance: Usually viral; rest, fluids, and warm steam inhalation help. Cough syrups with expectorants may assist. If fever is high or breathing becomes difficult, seek medical care. Bacterial tracheitis (more common in children) requires antibiotics and may need hospitalisation.
precautions: If you have a persistent cough, see a doctor

symptoms: production of clear or white sputum
guidance: Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and use a humidifier. Over-the-counter cough suppressants or expectorants may help. If coughing persists >3 weeks, or if you have high fever, shortness of breath, or blood in sputum, consult a doctor. Antibiotics are not effective for viral bronchitis. Avoid smoking.
precautions: If you have asthma, follow your asthma action plan

symptoms: triggered by changes in temperature, humidity, or strong odors
guidance: Avoid triggers such as perfumes, smoke, and temperature changes. Saline nasal rinses and intranasal corticosteroids can help. In some cases, antihistamines are not effective. See an ENT if symptoms are severe.
precautions: Keep nasal passages moist with saline sprays
If symptoms persist, consider allergy testing to rule out allergy

guidance: Treatment includes intranasal corticosteroids to shrink polyps. In severe cases, oral steroids or surgery (polypectomy) may be needed. Manage underlying allergies or asthma. Regular follow-up with an ENT is important.
precautions: If you have recurring polyps, consider allergy immunotherapy

symptoms: difficulty breathing through the nose (often one side)
guidance: Mild cases need no treatment. If symptoms are severe, septoplasty (surgical repair) may be recommended. This is a common condition. Medical management includes nasal decongestants and saline sprays.
precautions: If you have sleep apnea, treat it
Consult an ENT if breathing difficulty affects daily life

category: Vocal Cord Dysfunction (Paradoxical Vocal Fold Motion)
symptoms: triggered by exercise, stress, or irritants
guidance: This condition is often misdiagnosed as asthma. Speech therapy with breathing exercises is the main treatment. Avoid triggers and practice diaphragmatic breathing. An ENT or pulmonologist can diagnose with laryngoscopy.
precautions: If you have asthma, treat both conditions
Seek a specialist if symptoms persist

symptoms: feeling of a lump in the throat
guidance: Lifestyle changes: avoid acidic/spicy foods, eat small meals, avoid lying down after eating, elevate the head of the bed. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) may be prescribed. Persistent symptoms warrant an ENT or gastroenterologist consultation.
precautions: Elevate the head of your bed by 6-8 inches
Avoid trigger foods (citrus, tomato, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol)

symptoms: episodes of stopped breathing during sleep
guidance: Central sleep apnea is caused by the brain not sending signals to breathe. Treatment includes treating underlying conditions (heart failure, stroke), using adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) or CPAP, and oxygen therapy. Sleep study is diagnostic. Refer to a sleep specialist.
precautions: Avoid alcohol and sedatives before bed
If you have heart failure, manage it well
Follow up with sleep clinic regularly

symptoms: signs of right heart failure (edema, cyanosis) in advanced
guidance: This condition is defined by obesity, daytime hypoventilation (elevated PaCO2), and sleep-disordered breathing. Treatment: weight loss is the most effective. CPAP or BiPAP is used for sleep apnea. Ventilatory support may be needed. Refer to a pulmonologist.

symptoms: most commonly in infants <2 years, often due to RSV
guidance: This is a common viral lower respiratory infection in infants. Management is supportive: hydration, nasal suctioning, and oxygen if needed. Hospitalisation may be required if breathing difficulty or dehydration occurs. Do not use cough suppressants or antibiotics (unless bacterial superinfection). Prevention: handwashing and avoiding exposure to smoke.
precautions: Nasal saline drops and bulb suction to clear secretions
Seek emergency care if breathing becomes labored or bluish

symptoms: caused by inhalation of toxins (diacetyl, chemicals), post-infectious, or after lung transplant
guidance: This is a rare but severe obstructive lung disease. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms: bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and oxygen therapy. Lung transplant may be considered in advanced cases. Avoid exposure to causative agents. Early referral to a pulmonologist is essential.
precautions: Avoid occupational exposure to diacetyl and other harmful chemicals
Wear protective masks in high-risk environments
If you have a lung transplant, monitor closely

symptoms: progressive cough (dry or with scanty sputum)
similar to pneumonia but not responding to antibiotics
guidance: COP is a treatable interstitial pneumonia. Diagnosis is by biopsy (transbronchial or surgical). Treatment: corticosteroids (prednisolone) are the mainstay. Relapses are common. Management by a pulmonologist is essential. Do not delay diagnosis.
precautions: Take corticosteroids as prescribed and do not stop abruptly
Monitor for side effects (weight gain, hyperglycemia)
Regular follow-up with pulmonary function tests
Report any recurrence of symptoms promptly

guidance: Eosinophilic pneumonia is caused by allergens, drugs, or infections (including parasites). Treatment: corticosteroids (prednisolone) are highly effective. Identify and remove the cause (drugs, environmental triggers). Pulmonologist referral is needed.
precautions: If on steroids, follow the schedule strictly
Monitor for infections while on immunosuppression
Regular follow-up with chest X-ray and eosinophil count

symptoms: transient pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray
often associated with parasitic infections (Ascaris, hookworm), or drug reaction
guidance: This is a benign, self-limiting condition. Identify and treat the underlying cause (deworming for parasites, withdrawal of offending drug). In most cases, no specific treatment is needed. Symptomatic relief with antihistamines or corticosteroids if severe.
precautions: Good hygiene and handwashing (prevent parasitic infections)
Avoid self-medication with dewormers without diagnosis
If drug-induced, avoid the drug in the future
Seek medical advice if symptoms worsen

symptoms: common in tropical countries (India, Southeast Asia), caused by filarial infection
guidance: Diagnosis is by high eosinophil count and positive filarial serology. Treatment: diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is effective and available free under government programs. Corticosteroids may be added for severe symptoms. Prognosis is good with treatment.
precautions: Take the full course of DEC
If on steroids, follow the prescribed schedule

symptoms: often in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis
guidance: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus. Treatment: corticosteroids (prednisolone) and antifungal (itraconazole) to reduce fungal load. Monitoring of IgE levels and pulmonary function is essential. Pulmonologist management is required.
precautions: Use corticosteroids and antifungals as prescribed
Monitor for side effects of steroids
If you have asthma, manage it well

symptoms: acute: fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath hours after exposure
subacute: progressive cough, fatigue, weight loss
triggers: bird droppings (bird fancier's lung), mouldy hay (farmer's lung), etc.
guidance: Avoidance of the inciting antigen is the cornerstone. Corticosteroids for acute/subacute forms. Chronic HP may progress to fibrosis. Diagnosis requires high-resolution CT and sometimes biopsy. Pulmonologist referral is essential.
precautions: Identify and avoid the causative allergen
Use protective masks in high-risk occupations
Improve ventilation in work and living spaces
If you have chronic HP, consider lung transplant if severe
Regular follow-up with pulmonary function tests

symptoms: history of exposure to silica dust (mining, stone cutting, sandblasting)
guidance: Silicosis is preventable by dust control and use of respirators. There is no cure; treatment is supportive: bronchodilators, oxygen, and management of complications (TB, pneumothorax). Avoid further exposure. Free TB screening is available for silicosis patients.
precautions: Always wear approved respiratory protection in dust-prone jobs
If you have silicosis, get screened for TB

symptoms: history of asbestos exposure (mining, construction, shipbuilding)
guidance: There is no cure. Management is supportive: oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, and treatment of complications (pleural effusion, mesothelioma). Smoking cessation is crucial (synergistic effect with asbestos). Monitor for lung cancer and mesothelioma. Workers' compensation may be available.
precautions: If you work with asbestos, use appropriate protective equipment
Regular chest imaging and lung function tests
If you develop symptoms, seek medical attention immediately

guidance: Prevention is key through dust control. Treatment is supportive: bronchodilators, oxygen, and management of complications. Avoid further dust exposure. Regular surveillance of coal miners is recommended.
precautions: Use dust suppression measures in mines
If you have symptoms, seek medical evaluation

symptoms: history of beryllium exposure (aerospace, nuclear, electronics)
guidance: This is a granulomatous lung disease similar to sarcoidosis. Diagnosis: beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT). Treatment: corticosteroids and immunosuppressants. Avoid further exposure. Screening for exposed workers is essential.
precautions: Use protective equipment in high-risk jobs
If diagnosed, follow pulmonary care closely

symptoms: history of welding or iron dust exposure
benign, often reversible with cessation of exposure
guidance: Siderosis is generally benign and does not progress to fibrosis. The main treatment is removal from exposure. Pulmonary function is usually normal. Regular monitoring is recommended.
precautions: Ensure adequate ventilation in the workplace
If you have symptoms, consult a pulmonologist

symptoms: history of tin mining or smelting
guidance: Stannosis is benign and does not cause significant lung impairment. Removal from exposure is sufficient. No specific treatment is needed.
precautions: Use dust control measures in tin-related industries
If symptoms occur, rule out other causes

symptoms: history of talc mining or industrial use
guidance: Talcosis can cause fibrosis. Treatment is supportive: bronchodilators, oxygen, and avoidance of further exposure. In severe cases, lung transplant may be considered. Regular monitoring is important.

symptoms: worse on the first day of the work week (Monday morning chest)
history of working with cotton, flax, or hemp
guidance: Byssinosis is an occupational lung disease. Prevention: dust control in textile mills. Treatment: bronchodilators and corticosteroids may help. Avoidance of further exposure is key. If severe, consider changing occupation.
precautions: Improve ventilation and dust control at work
If symptoms persist, seek medical advice
Regular health checkups for textile workers

symptoms: history of exposure to mouldy sugar cane bagasse
guidance: This is a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Avoidance of bagasse dust is essential. Corticosteroids may be needed in acute cases. Diagnosis is by history and imaging. Supportive care.
precautions: Improve drying and storage to prevent mould
If symptoms develop, seek medical care

symptoms: Lofgren's syndrome (fever, erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy)
guidance: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease. Treatment: corticosteroids are first-line; immunosuppressants for refractory cases. Many cases resolve spontaneously. Regular follow-up with pulmonary function tests and imaging is needed. Eye and cardiac involvement require specialist care.
precautions: Take steroids as prescribed and taper slowly
If you have cardiac symptoms, see a cardiologist

guidance: PAP is a rare disease caused by accumulation of surfactant. Treatment: whole-lung lavage (bronchoalveolar lavage) is the standard. In some cases, GM-CSF therapy. Referral to a specialist centre is essential.
precautions: If you have unexplained dyspnoea and crazy-paving CT, suspect PAP
Whole-lung lavage is safe and effective
Follow up with pulmonary function tests

symptoms: cystic lesions on CT, often in young adult smokers
guidance: PLCH is associated with smoking in most cases. Smoking cessation is the main treatment; many cases improve. Corticosteroids may be used if progressive. In severe cases, lung transplant. Close monitoring with PFTs and CT.
precautions: If you have recurrent pneumothorax, seek care

symptoms: occurs almost exclusively in women of childbearing age
guidance: LAM is a rare cystic lung disease. Treatment: sirolimus (rapamycin) has been shown to stabilise lung function. Bronchodilators and oxygen therapy. Lung transplant for end-stage. Referral to a LAM specialist centre is essential.
precautions: Monitor for pneumothorax – seek care immediately for sudden chest pain
If you have angiomyolipomas, monitor for rupture

symptoms: recurrent infections (pneumonia) in the same area
may be asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging
congenital anomaly with non-functional lung tissue
guidance: Diagnosis is by CT angiography. Treatment: surgical resection if symptomatic or recurrent infections. Asymptomatic cases may be monitored. Referral to a thoracic surgeon is needed.
precautions: If you have recurrent pneumonia, seek workup for sequestration

symptoms: if large, may cause cough, dyspnoea, or wheezing
guidance: Bronchogenic cysts are congenital. If asymptomatic, they can be observed. If symptomatic or infected, surgical excision is recommended. Endoscopic drainage may be an option.
precautions: If you have recurrent chest infections, rule out cyst
Surgical removal is safe and curative

symptoms: cystic lung lesion on prenatal ultrasound
guidance: CCAM is a congenital lung malformation. Management: asymptomatic cases may be observed; if symptomatic or large, surgical resection is recommended. Prenatal diagnosis is common. Paediatric pulmonology and surgical consultation are needed.
precautions: If diagnosed prenatally, plan delivery in a centre with paediatric surgery
If recurrent infections, surgery is curative

symptoms: epistaxis (nosebleeds) – may be associated with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT)
guidance: PAVMs are abnormal communications between pulmonary arteries and veins. Treatment: endovascular embolisation is the treatment of choice. Screening for HHT is important. If large or symptomatic, intervention is needed.
precautions: If you have unexplained cyanosis or clubbing, seek evaluation
If you have HHT, screen for PAVMs

symptoms: signs of right heart failure (oedema, jugular venous distension)
guidance: PVOD is a rare cause of pulmonary hypertension. Diagnosis is by right heart catheterisation and imaging (septal lines). Treatment: supportive, and lung transplant is the only curative option. Avoid vasodilators (may cause pulmonary oedema). Referral to a PH centre is essential.
precautions: Avoid medications that can worsen (some vasodilators)
If you have pulmonary hypertension with risk factors, suspect PVOD
Regular follow-up with a PH specialist

guidance: PCH is a rare disease with proliferation of pulmonary capillaries. Treatment is limited; lung transplant is the only option. Diagnosis by lung biopsy. Palliative care for advanced cases.
precautions: If you have unexplained pulmonary hypertension with haemoptysis, consider PCH
Refer to a PH expert centre

guidance: This is a weakness of the tracheal wall. Treatment: continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or stenting in severe cases. In children, it may resolve with growth. Avoid irritants. Pulmonary rehabilitation.
precautions: If you have recurrent infections, seek evaluation
In severe cases, consult a pulmonologist
Maintain good hydration to keep secretions thin

symptoms: history of intubation, trauma, or infection
guidance: Tracheal stenosis is a narrowing of the trachea. Treatment: bronchoscopic dilatation, stent placement, or surgical resection. Referral to a thoracic surgeon or pulmonologist is essential. Avoid further airway trauma.
precautions: If you have had prolonged intubation, monitor for stridor

guidance: Bronchomalacia is a weakness of the bronchial walls. Treatment: supportive (physiotherapy, bronchodilators), and in severe cases, stenting or surgery. Avoid triggers and smoke. Follow-up with a pulmonologist.
precautions: In children, may improve with age

symptoms: after lung or bone marrow transplant
guidance: This is a form of chronic rejection after lung transplant. Treatment: augmented immunosuppression, azithromycin, and possibly retransplantation in selected cases. Early detection with PFTs is crucial. Multidisciplinary care.
precautions: If you have a transplant, report any decline in breathing

category: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (Chronic Lung Disease of Prematurity)
symptoms: need for oxygen therapy beyond 36 weeks postmenstrual age
guidance: BPD is a complication of premature birth and mechanical ventilation. Management: oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, diuretics, and nutrition support. Prevention: antenatal steroids, gentle ventilation. Long-term follow-up for pulmonary function and developmental issues.
precautions: Prevent premature birth with good antenatal care
If your baby has BPD, follow the NICU team's advice

symptoms: reduced breath sounds on the affected side
guidance: Atelectasis is collapse of lung tissue. It can be caused by obstruction (mucus plug, tumour), compression (pleural effusion), or surgery. Treatment: deep breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, bronchodilators, and treatment of underlying cause. If severe, bronchoscopy may be needed.
precautions: After surgery, do deep breathing exercises
If you have a tumour, treat it

symptoms: sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing
pain may be relieved by lying on the affected side
guidance: Pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura. Treatment: NSAIDs for pain; treat the underlying cause (infection, autoimmune, or PE). Rest and deep breathing exercises. If pain is severe or associated with breathlessness, seek medical care.
precautions: If you have a fever, see a doctor

symptoms: causes: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
guidance: Transudative effusion is due to systemic factors. Treatment: manage the underlying cause (diuretics for heart failure). If large and symptomatic, therapeutic thoracentesis. Do not ignore if recurrent.
precautions: If you have heart failure, take diuretics as prescribed

symptoms: causes: pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, autoimmune
guidance: Exudative effusion requires diagnostic thoracentesis to identify the cause. Treatment: antibiotics for infection, chemotherapy for malignancy, or treatment of the underlying condition. Large effusions may need drainage.
precautions: If you have fever and pleural effusion, it could be empyema

guidance: Empyema is a serious infection of the pleural space. Treatment: antibiotics, chest tube drainage, and sometimes surgery (decortication). Hospitalisation is required. Do not delay; empyema can be life-threatening.
precautions: Seek immediate care if you have fever and pleural effusion
If you have pneumonia, follow up to ensure it resolves

symptoms: often due to trauma, malignancy, or lymphatic obstruction
guidance: Chylothorax is a leakage of chyle into the pleural space. Treatment: dietary modification (low-fat, high-MCT diet), octreotide, and sometimes surgery (thoracic duct ligation). Treat the underlying cause. Fluid drainage may be needed.
precautions: Follow a low-fat diet with MCT oil
If you have trauma, monitor for chylothorax
Surgery may be needed if refractory
Regular follow-up with a thoracic surgeon

guidance: Hemothorax is blood in the pleural space, usually from trauma. Treatment: chest tube drainage and blood transfusion if needed. Urgent surgical consultation if ongoing bleeding. Do not delay; it can be life-threatening.
precautions: If you have chest trauma, seek emergency care
If on anticoagulants, inform the team
Prepare for surgery if bleeding continues

symptoms: pleural fluid cytology positive for malignant cells
guidance: Management: therapeutic thoracentesis for symptom relief, pleurodesis (talc) to prevent reaccumulation, and treatment of the underlying cancer. Palliative care may be needed. Referral to oncology.
precautions: If you have cancer and develop shortness of breath, seek care

symptoms: occurs in young, tall, thin individuals without underlying lung disease
guidance: Small pneumothoraces may resolve with observation and oxygen therapy. Large or symptomatic ones require needle aspiration or chest tube insertion. Recurrence is common; pleurodesis may be considered after the second episode. Avoid flying and diving until resolved.
precautions: Seek emergency care for sudden chest pain with breathlessness
If you have had a pneumothorax, avoid flying and diving
Do not smoke – increases recurrence risk
If you have recurrent pneumothorax, consider pleurodesis

symptoms: underlying lung disease (COPD, cystic fibrosis, interstitial lung disease)
guidance: This is more serious and often requires chest tube drainage. Hospitalisation is needed. Treat the underlying disease. Recurrence is high; pleurodesis is often recommended. Do not delay treatment.
precautions: If you have chronic lung disease and develop sudden breathlessness, seek emergency care
Manage your underlying lung disease optimally

guidance: Mesothelioma is a rare and aggressive cancer. Treatment: surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and immunotherapy. Early diagnosis improves outcomes. Referral to a specialist centre is essential. Asbestos exposure is the main risk factor.
precautions: If you have been exposed, get regular checkups
If you have symptoms, seek immediate evaluation

symptoms: found incidentally on chest X-ray or CT
may be a granuloma, hamartoma, or infection
guidance: Most pulmonary nodules are benign. Management: follow-up CT scans to monitor growth. If large, suspicious, or growing, biopsy or surgery may be needed. Do not panic; most are not cancer. Regular monitoring is key.
precautions: If you have a family history of lung cancer, discuss with your doctor

symptoms: rarely causes cough or pain if large
guidance: Hamartomas are benign tumours composed of cartilage, fat, and connective tissue. They do not become malignant. If symptomatic or growing, surgical removal may be considered. No treatment needed for asymptomatic ones.
precautions: If you have symptoms, discuss with a pulmonologist

symptoms: history of taking drugs (amiodarone, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, etc.)
guidance: Stop the offending drug immediately. Corticosteroids may be needed. Pulmonary function and imaging monitoring is essential. Referral to a pulmonologist. Prognosis depends on the drug and severity.
precautions: If you are on a drug known to cause pulmonary fibrosis, report any breathlessness
Regular lung function tests during therapy with such drugs
Do not stop medications without consulting your doctor

symptoms: occurs 1-6 months after radiation therapy to the chest (for breast, lung, or lymphoma)
guidance: Treatment: corticosteroids (prednisolone) are the mainstay. In severe cases, oxygen and supportive care. Prevention: modern radiation techniques reduce the risk. Patients should report symptoms promptly.
precautions: If you have had chest radiation, monitor for new cough or dyspnoea
Regular follow-up with oncology and pulmonology
If symptoms are severe, seek emergency care

symptoms: interstitial lung disease (usual interstitial pneumonia pattern)
guidance: Lung involvement is common in RA. Management: treat RA with DMARDs/biologics; corticosteroids for acute exacerbations. Pulmonary function tests and HRCT monitoring. Smoking cessation. Multidisciplinary care with rheumatology and pulmonology.
precautions: If you have RA and develop breathlessness, see a pulmonologist

symptoms: signs of SLE (malar rash, arthritis, nephritis)
guidance: Lupus pneumonitis is a rare but serious manifestation of SLE. Treatment: corticosteroids and immunosuppressants. Hospitalisation may be needed. Monitor for respiratory failure. Optimise SLE therapy.
precautions: If you have SLE and develop respiratory symptoms, see a doctor
Regular follow-up with rheumatologist and pulmonologist

guidance: ILD is a major cause of death in scleroderma. Treatment: immunosuppressants (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide) and antifibrotics (nintedanib). Pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen therapy. Referral to a scleroderma centre.
precautions: Early diagnosis with PFTs and HRCT

guidance: Sjogren's can affect the lungs. Treatment: bronchodilators, mucolytics, and immunosuppression for ILD. Good hydration and humidification. Regular dental care (dry mouth). Referral to pulmonologist.
precautions: If you have recurrent infections, consider bronchiectasis

guidance: ILD can be the presenting feature. Treatment: corticosteroids and immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide). Rapidly progressive forms may need aggressive therapy. Multidisciplinary management.
precautions: If you have muscle weakness and breathlessness, seek evaluation

guidance: This is a rare autoimmune disease affecting lungs and kidneys. Treatment: plasmapheresis, corticosteroids, and cyclophosphamide. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent renal failure. Referral to nephrology and pulmonology.
precautions: If you have hemoptysis and blood in urine, seek immediate care

guidance: This is a vasculitis affecting small vessels. Treatment: corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab. Early treatment can induce remission. Multidisciplinary care (rheumatology, pulmonology, nephrology).
precautions: If you have sinusitis and lung lesions, consider GPA

guidance: Treatment is similar to GPA: corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide/rituximab. Early recognition prevents organ damage. Multidisciplinary care is essential.
precautions: If you have pulmonary and renal symptoms, seek immediate care

guidance: This is a vasculitis with eosinophilic infiltration. Treatment: corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide/rituximab. Omalizumab may help in some cases. Multidisciplinary care.
precautions: If you have asthma with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, suspect EGPA

symptoms: may be part of systemic vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA)
guidance: Treatment depends on the underlying vasculitis: immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, rituximab) and corticosteroids. Early diagnosis is crucial. Referral to rheumatology and pulmonology.
precautions: If you have unexplained respiratory symptoms with systemic signs, seek evaluation

guidance: Treatment: corticosteroids are the mainstay; immunosuppressants may be needed. Iron supplementation for anemia. Avoid triggers (if known). Referral to a pulmonologist. Prognosis varies.
precautions: If you have recurrent hemoptysis, seek evaluation

symptoms: diffuse alveolar infiltrates on chest imaging
guidance: Alveolar hemorrhage is a medical emergency. Causes include vasculitis, Goodpasture, and drug reactions. Treatment: high-dose corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and supportive care. Bronchoscopy and BAL are diagnostic. Urgent management is needed.
precautions: If you have a known systemic disease, report symptoms

symptoms: signs of underlying vasculitis or autoimmune disease
guidance: DAH is a life-threatening emergency. Immediate hospitalisation, high-dose corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants are needed. Bronchoscopy with BAL will show progressively bloodier returns. Plasmapheresis may be used. ICU support is often required.
precautions: Do not delay – DAH can be fatal
If you have systemic symptoms, report them

guidance: This is a medical emergency. Diagnosis: anti-GBM, ANCA, and renal biopsy. Treatment: plasmapheresis, steroids, cyclophosphamide, and dialysis. Early referral to nephrology and pulmonology is critical.
precautions: If you have both lung and kidney symptoms, seek emergency care

guidance: This is a genetic cause of emphysema. Treatment: smoking cessation is the most important. Augmentation therapy with intravenous AAT is available (free under some programs). Bronchodilators and pulmonary rehabilitation. Genetic counselling for family members.
precautions: If you have early-onset COPD, get tested for AAT deficiency

symptoms: history of recurrent respiratory infections from childhood
guidance: This is a genetic disorder affecting ciliary motility. Diagnosis: nasal nitric oxide, electron microscopy of cilia, or genetic testing. Management: chest physiotherapy, bronchodilators, antibiotics for infections, and ENT care. Avoid smoking. Multidisciplinary care.
precautions: Regular chest physiotherapy to clear secretions

guidance: This is a rare disorder. Treatment: supportive; vitamin E and zinc may help nails. Pleural effusion may need drainage. Treat underlying conditions (if any). No specific cure.
precautions: Maintain good skin and nail care

guidance: This is a rare condition of dilated lymphatics. Treatment: supportive, including oxygen, drainage of pleural effusion, and dietary modification (MCT oil). In severe cases, surgical intervention. Paediatric pulmonology care.
precautions: If your child has respiratory distress, seek specialist care

guidance: This is a complication of positive pressure ventilation in premature infants. Management: conservative with lower pressures, oxygen, and sometimes selective bronchial intubation. Prevention: gentle ventilation strategies. Paediatric intensivist care.
precautions: If your baby has PIE, follow NICU advice

symptoms: may be asymptomatic and discovered later
guidance: This is a congenital anomaly causing overinflation of a lung lobe. Treatment: surgical resection (lobectomy) if symptomatic. Asymptomatic cases may be observed. Paediatric surgery referral.
precautions: If your child has breathing difficulty, seek evaluation

symptoms: absence of one or both lungs
guidance: This is a rare congenital absence of lung tissue. Treatment: supportive; may need long-term ventilation. Prognosis depends on the extent and associated anomalies. Multidisciplinary care.

symptoms: scimitar sign on chest X-ray (curvilinear shadow)
associated with anomalous pulmonary venous return
guidance: This is a rare congenital anomaly. Treatment: if symptomatic, surgical repair of anomalous venous return or embolisation of collaterals. Asymptomatic cases can be followed. Multidisciplinary care.
precautions: If you have recurrent infections, consider surgery

guidance: This is a congenital vascular anomaly where the left pulmonary artery originates from the right. Treatment: surgical reimplantation is needed if symptomatic. Early diagnosis is key. Referral to paediatric cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery.
precautions: If your child has stridor and feeding difficulties, seek evaluation

symptoms: incidental finding of a bronchocoele (mucus-filled cyst)
associated with hyperlucency of a segment
guidance: This is a congenital defect where a segmental bronchus is occluded. If asymptomatic, observation. If recurrent infections, surgical resection. Diagnosis by CT. Pulmonology and thoracic surgery review.
precautions: If you have recurrent infections, consider surgery
Monitor for growth of the cyst

symptoms: inspiratory stridor (high-pitched) in infants, usually from birth
worse with crying, feeding, or lying on the back
rarely causes feeding difficulty or cyanosis
guidance: This is the most common cause of stridor in infants. Most cases are benign and self-limiting. If the infant has feeding problems, poor weight gain, or cyanosis, evaluation by ENT is needed. Severe cases may need supraglottoplasty.
precautions: Keep the infant upright during feeds
If breathing difficulty or cyanosis, seek emergency care

symptoms: caused by nerve damage (surgery, tumour, viral)
guidance: Treatment: voice therapy, and if severe, surgical interventions (injection laryngoplasty, thyroplasty). Bilateral paralysis may cause airway obstruction – emergency tracheostomy may be needed. ENT specialist evaluation is essential.
precautions: If you have sudden voice loss after surgery, see an ENT

symptoms: slow-growing benign warts in the larynx, caused by HPV (types 6, 11)
guidance: Treatment: surgical removal (microdebrider, laser) is the mainstay. Adjuvant therapy: interferon, cidofovir, or bevacizumab may reduce recurrence. HPV vaccination is preventive. Regular ENT follow-up.
precautions: If you have recurring hoarseness, see an ENT

symptoms: history of smoking and alcohol use
guidance: Early diagnosis is key – if hoarseness persists, get a laryngoscopy. Treatment: surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy depending on stage. Early-stage cancer has a good prognosis. Smoking cessation is the best prevention.
precautions: If hoarseness lasts >3 weeks, see an ENT

guidance: Most are self-limiting. Rest, hydration, and symptomatic relief (paracetamol, cough syrup). See a doctor if fever >3 days, shortness of breath, or worsening symptoms. Handwashing prevents spread.
precautions: If you have underlying lung disease, seek care earlier

symptoms: worse with movement or deep breathing
guidance: This is inflammation of the cartilage connecting ribs to the breastbone. Treatment: NSAIDs, heat application, and rest. Reassurance is important. If pain is severe or associated with shortness of breath, rule out cardiac causes.
precautions: If chest pain is new, get cardiac evaluation
Do not ignore if pain is accompanied by other symptoms

guidance: Pulmonary infarction is lung tissue death due to obstruction of pulmonary blood supply, usually from PE. Treatment: anticoagulation for PE, supportive care, and oxygen. If large, may need thrombolysis. Emergency care is needed.
precautions: If you have chest pain with hemoptysis, seek emergency
If you have risk factors for DVT/PE, use prophylaxis

symptoms: often due to trauma, central venous catheter, or scuba diving
guidance: This is a medical emergency. Treatment: position the patient in Trendelenburg (head down, left lateral) to trap air in the right ventricle. High-flow oxygen. If possible, hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Emergency intervention is needed.
precautions: Invasive procedures: ensure air is purged from lines
If you have a central line, monitor for air
If symptoms develop after line manipulation, seek immediate care

symptoms: occurs with rapid changes in pressure (scuba diving, mechanical ventilation)
guidance: Barotrauma is lung injury from pressure changes. Treatment: oxygen, chest tube for pneumothorax, and supportive care. If on a ventilator, reduce pressures. Divers should ascend slowly. Emergency care is needed.
precautions: If you are diving, ascend slowly
Do not hold your breath during ascent
If you have lung disease, consult a doctor before diving
If symptoms occur, seek medical care
Avoid flying if you have a pneumothorax

category: Diving-Related Pulmonary Disorder (e.g., Pulmonary Overinflation Syndrome)
symptoms: after scuba diving with rapid ascent
guidance: This is a type of barotrauma. Treatment: oxygen, observation, and chest tube if needed. Avoid diving if you have lung cysts or asthma. Emergency evaluation is required.
precautions: Do not dive if you have a respiratory infection
If you have a history of pneumothorax, avoid diving

category: High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE) – Prevention and Management
symptoms: dry cough progressing to frothy sputum
guidance: Descend immediately – this is the most important treatment. Administer oxygen if available. Nifedipine and dexamethasone may be used. Portable hyperbaric bags can be life-saving. Ascend slowly with acclimatisation.
precautions: Avoid alcohol and sedatives at high altitude
If symptoms, descend – do not wait
Take acetazolamide for prophylaxis if susceptible
Know the signs – early recognition saves lives

category: High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE) – Prevention and Management
guidance: This is a medical emergency. Descend immediately. Give dexamethasone and oxygen. If descent is not possible, use a hyperbaric bag. Do not leave the person alone.
precautions: If you have HAPE, treat aggressively
Know the symptoms – early descent is life-saving

symptoms: occurs after rapid decompression in divers or aviators
guidance: Treatment: recompression in a hyperbaric chamber is the definitive treatment. Administer 100% oxygen. Do not fly after diving. Emergency transport to a hyperbaric facility is needed.
precautions: Do not fly within 12-24 hours after diving
Do not ignore – can be fatal

symptoms: history of repeated exposure to organic antigens (birds, mouldy hay)
guidance: Treatment: avoidance of the antigen is the most important. Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants may slow progression. In advanced cases, lung transplant may be considered. Management by a pulmonologist is essential.
precautions: Identify and avoid the causative antigen
If you have bird exposure, remove birds
